entries.d64a350d012a05edfc96bbda26e608b4d0d7bc5a: <div sID="gen6136" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="2Sam.10" sID="2Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen6136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6137" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6138" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives us an account of a war David has with the Ammonites and the Syrians their allies, with the occasion and success of it. I. David sent a friendly embassy to Hanun king of the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He, upon a base surmise that it was ill intended, abused David's ambassadors, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3-2Sam.10.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. David resenting it (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">ver. 5</reference>), and the Ammonites prepared for war against him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. David carried the war into their country, sent against them. Joab and Abishai, who addressed themselves to the battle with a great deal of conduct and bravery, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7-2Sam.10.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. V. The Ammonites, and the Syrians their allies, were totally routed, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.13-2Sam.10.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. VI. The forces of the Syrians, which rallied again, were a second time defeated, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.15-2Sam.10.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. Thus did David advance his own reputation for gratitude, in returning kindness, and for justice, in repaying injuries.
entries.49bc6c8fb03e4b9316d1fe81be6b1b669812a062: <div eID="gen6138" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6137" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Hanun's Usage of David's Servants. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1038.)</title> <div sID="gen6139" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass after this, that the king of the children of Ammon died, and Hanun his son reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants for his father. And David's servants came into the land of the children of Ammon. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the princes of the children of Ammon said unto Hanun their lord, Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? hath not David <hi type="italic">rather</hi> sent his servants unto thee, to search the city, and to spy it out, and to overthrow it? <hi type="super">4</hi> Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to their buttocks, and sent them away. <hi type="super">5</hi> When they told <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto David, he sent to meet them, because the men were greatly ashamed: and the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and <hi type="italic">then</hi> return. <div eID="gen6139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6140" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The great respect David paid to his neighbour, the king of the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. 1. The inducement to it was some kindness he had formerly received from Nahash the deceased king. He <hi type="italic">showed kindness to me,</hi> says David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.2">v. 2</reference>), and therefore (having lately had satisfaction in showing kindness to Mephibosheth for his father's sake) he resolves to show kindness to his son, and to keep up a friendly correspondence with him. Thus the pleasure of doing one kind and generous action should excite us to another. Nahash had been an enemy to Israel, a cruel enemy (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1 Sam. xi. 2</reference>), and yet had shown kindness to David, perhaps only in contradiction to Saul, who was unkind to him: however, if David receives kindness, he is not nice in examining the grounds and principles of it, but resolves gratefully to return it. If a Pharisee give alms in pride, though God will not reward him, yet he that receives the alms ought to return thanks for it. God knows the heart, but we do not. 2. The particular instance of respect was sending an embassy to condole with him on his father's death, as is common among princes in alliance with each other: <hi type="italic">David sent to comfort him.</hi> Note, It is a comfort to children, when their parents are dead, to find that their parents' friends are theirs, and that they intend to keep up an acquaintance with them. It is a comfort to mourners to find that there are those who mourn with them, are sensible of their loss and share with them in it. It is a comfort to those who are honouring the memory of their deceased relations to find there are others who likewise honour it and who had a value for those whom they valued. <div eID="gen6140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6141" type="x-p"/> II. The great affront which Hanun the king of the Ammonites put upon David in his ambassadors. 1. He hearkened to the spiteful suggestions of his princes, who insinuated that David's ambassadors, under pretence of being comforters, were sent as spies, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">v. 3</reference>. False men are ready to think others as false as themselves; and those that bear ill-will to their neighbours are resolved not to believe that their neighbours bear any good-will to them. They would not thus have imagined that David dissembled but that they were conscious to themselves that they could have dissembled, to serve a turn. Unfounded suspicion argues a wicked mind. Bishop Patrick's note on this is that "there is nothing so well meant but it may be ill interpreted, and is wont to be so by men who love nobody but themselves." Men of the greatest honour and virtue must not think it strange if they be thus misrepresented. <hi type="italic">Charity thinketh no evil.</hi> 2. Entertaining this vile suggestion, he basely abused David's ambassadors, like a man of a sordid villainous spirit, that was fitter to rake a kennel than to wear a crown. If he had any reason to suspect that David's messengers came on a bad design, he would have done prudently enough to be upon the reserve with them, and to dismiss them as soon as he could; but it is plain he only sought an occasion to put the utmost disgrace he could upon them, out of an antipathy to their king and their country. They were themselves men of honour, and much more so as they represented the prince that sent them; they and their reputation were under the special protection of the law of nations; they put a confidence in the Ammonites, and came among them unarmed; yet Hanun used them like rogues and vagabonds, and worse, <hi type="italic">shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the midst,</hi> to expose them to the contempt and ridicule of his servants, that they might make sport with them and that these men might seem vile. <div eID="gen6141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6142" type="x-p"/> III. David's tender concern for his servants that were thus abused. He sent to meet them, and to let them know how much he interested himself in their quarrel and how soon he would avenge it, and directed them to stay at Jericho, a private place, where they would not have occasion to come into company, till that half of their beards which was shaved off had grown to such a length that the other half might be decently cut to it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">v. 5</reference>. The Jews wore their beards long, reckoning it an honour to appear aged and grave; and therefore it was not fit that persons of their rank and figure should appear at court unlike their neighbours. Change of raiment, it is likely, they had with them, to put on, instead of that which was cut off; but the loss of their beards would not be so soon repaired; yet in time these would grow again, and all would be well. Let us learn not to lay too much to heart unjust reproaches; after awhile they will wear off of themselves, and turn only to the shame of their authors, while the injured reputation in a little time grows again, as these beards did. God will <hi type="italic">bring forth thy righteousness as the light,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">wait patiently for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6-Ps.37.7">Ps. xxxvii. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen6142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6143" type="x-p"/> Some have thought that David, in the indignity he received from the king of Ammon, was but well enough served for courting and complimenting that pagan prince, whom he knew to be an inveterate enemy to Israel, and might now remember how, when he would have put out the right eyes of the men of Jabesh-Gilead, he designed that, as he did this, for a <hi type="italic">reproach upon all Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1 Sam. xi. 2</reference>. What better usage could he expect from such a spiteful family and people? Why should he covet the friendship of a people whom Israel must have so little to do with as that an Ammonite might not <hi type="italic">enter into the congregation of the Lord, even to the tenth generation?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>.
entries.7fb7e2b54520caad5505ca6a9514411f9aa34e57: <div eID="gen6143" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Ammonites and Syrians Defeated. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1037.)</title> <div sID="gen6144" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zoba, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when David heard of <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array at the entering in of the gate: and the Syrians of Zoba, and of Rehob, and Ishtob, and Maacah, <hi type="italic">were</hi> by themselves in the field. <hi type="super">9</hi> When Joab saw that the front of the battle was against him before and behind, he chose of all the choice <hi type="italic">men</hi> of Israel, and put <hi type="italic">them</hi> in array against the Syrians: <hi type="super">10</hi> And the rest of the people he delivered into the hand of Abishai his brother, that he might put <hi type="italic">them</hi> in array against the children of Ammon. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he said, If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will come and help thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do that which seemeth him good. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Joab drew nigh, and the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, unto the battle against the Syrians: and they fled before him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, then fled they also before Abishai, and entered into the city. So Joab returned from the children of Ammon, and came to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen6144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6145" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The preparation which the Ammonites made for war, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">v. 6</reference>. They saw they had made themselves very odious to David and obnoxious to his just displeasure. This they might easily have foreseen when they abused his ambassadors, which was no other than a challenge to war, and a bold defiance of him. Yet, it seems, they had not considered how unable they were, with their thousands, to meet his; for now they found themselves an unequal match, and were forced to hire forces of other nations into their service. Thus sinners daringly provoke God, and expose themselves to his wrath, and never consider that he is <hi type="italic">stronger than they,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.22">1 Cor. x. 22</reference>. The Ammonites gave the affront first, and they were the first that raised forces to justify it. Had they humbled themselves, and begged David's pardon, probably an honorary satisfaction might have atoned for the offence. But, when they were thus desperately resolved to stand by what they had done, they courted their own ruin. <div eID="gen6145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6146" type="x-p"/> II. The speedy descent which David's forces made upon them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7">v. 7</reference>. When David heard of their military preparations, he sent Joab with a great army to attack them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7">v. 7</reference>. Those that are at war with the Son of David not only give the provocation, but begin the war; for he <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">strengthen themselves against him,</hi> and therefore, <hi type="italic">if they turn not, he will whet his sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.12">Ps. vii. 12</reference>. God has forces to send against those that set his wrath at defiance (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa. v. 19</reference>), which will convince them, when it is too late, that <hi type="italic">none ever hardened his heart against God and prospered.</hi> It was David's prudence to carry the war into their country, and fight them at the entering in of the gate of their capital city, <hi type="italic">Rabbah,</hi> as some think, or <hi type="italic">Medeba,</hi> a city in their borders, before which they pitched to guard their coast, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1 Chron. xix. 7</reference>. Such are the terrors and desolations of war that every good prince will, in love to his people, keep it as much as may be at a distance from them. <div eID="gen6146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> III. Preparations made on both sides for an engagement. 1. The enemy disposed themselves into two bodies, one of Ammonites, which, being their own, were posted at the gate of the city; the other of Syrians, whom they had taken into their pay, and who were therefore posted at a distance in the field, to charge the forces of Israel in the flank or rear, while the Ammonites charged them in the front, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.8">v. 8</reference>. 2. Joab, like a wise general, was soon aware of the design, and accordingly divided his forces: the choicest men he took under his own command, to fight the Syrians, whom probably he knew to be the better soldiers, and, being hired men, better versed in the arts of war, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.9">v. 9</reference>. The rest of the forces he put under the command of Abishai his brother, to engage the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.10">v. 10</reference>. It should seem, Joab found the enemy so well prepared to receive them that his conduct and courage were never so tried as now. <div eID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6148" type="x-p"/> IV. Joab's speech before the battle, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.11-2Sam.10.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. It is not long, but pertinent, and brave. 1. He prudently concerts the matter with Abishai his brother, that the dividing of the forces might not be the weakening of them, but that, which part soever was borne hard upon, the other should come in to its assistance. He supposes the worst, that one of them should be obliged to give back; and in that case, upon a signal given, the other should send a detachment to relieve it. Note, Mutual helpfulness is brotherly duty. If occasion be, <hi type="italic">thou shalt help me, and I will help thee.</hi> Christ's soldiers should thus strengthen one another's hands in their spiritual warfare. The strong must succour and help the weak. Those that through grace are conquerors over temptation must counsel, and comfort, and pray for, those that are tempted. <hi type="italic">When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>. The members of the natural body help one another, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1 Cor. xii. 21</reference>. 2. He bravely encourages himself, and his brother, and the rest of the officers and soldiers, to do their utmost. Great dangers put an edge upon true courage. When Joab saw the front of the battle was against him, both before and behind, instead of giving orders to make an honourable retreat, he animated his men to charge so much more furiously: <hi type="italic">Be of good courage and let us play the men,</hi> not for pay and preferment, for honour and fame, but <hi type="italic">for our people, and for the cities of our God,</hi> for the public safety and welfare, in which the glory of God is so much interested. <hi type="italic">God and our country</hi> was the word. "Let us be valiant, from a principle of love to Israel, that are our people, descended from the same stock, for whom we are employed, and in whose peace we shall have peace; and from a principle of love to God, for they are his cities that we are fighting in the defence of." The relation which any person or thing stands in to God should endear it to us, and engage us to do our utmost in its service. 3. He piously leaves the issue with God: "When we have done our part, according to the duty of our place, <hi type="italic">let the Lord do that which seemeth to him good.</hi>" Let nothing be wanting in us, whatever the success be; let God's work be done by us, and then God's will be done concerning us. When we make conscience of doing our duty we may, with the greatest satisfaction, leave the event with God, not thinking that our valour binds him to prosper us, but that still he may do as he pleases, yet hoping for his salvation in his own way and time. <div eID="gen6148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6149" type="x-p"/> V. The victory Joab obtained over the confederate forces of Syria and Ammon, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.13-2Sam.10.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. He provided for the worst, and put the case that the Syrians and Ammonites might prove too strong for him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.11">v. 11</reference>), but he proved too strong for them both. We do not hinder our success by preparing for disappointment. The Syrians were first routed by Joab, and then the Ammonites by Abishai; the Ammonites seem not to have fought at all, but, upon the retreat of the Syrians, to have fled into the city. It is a temptation to soldiers to fly when they have a city at their backs to fly to. It is one thing when men may either fight or fly and another thing when they must either fight or die.
entries.a1c2e0704b0eddee45f74a60435ec930baef9096: <div eID="gen6149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6150" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And when the Syrians saw that they were smitten before Israel, they gathered themselves together. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Hadarezer sent, and brought out the Syrians that <hi type="italic">were</hi> beyond the river: and they came to Helam; and Shobach the captain of the host of Hadarezer <hi type="italic">went</hi> before them. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together, and passed over Jordan, and came to Helam. And the Syrians set themselves in array against David, and fought with him. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew <hi type="italic">the men of</hi> seven hundred chariots of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when all the kings <hi type="italic">that were</hi> servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them. So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more. <div eID="gen6150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6151" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A new attempt of the Syrians to recover their lost honour and to check the progress of David's victorious arms. The forces that were lately dispersed rallied again, and <hi type="italic">gathered themselves together,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.15">v. 15</reference>. Even the baffled cause will make head as long as there is any life in it; the enemies of the Son of David do so, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.34">Matt, xxii. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.19">Rev. xix. 19</reference>. These, being conscious of their insufficiency, called in the aid of their allies and dependencies on the other side of <hi type="italic">the river</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">v. 16</reference>), and, being thus recruited, they hoped to make their part good against Israel, but <hi type="italic">they knew not the thoughts of the Lord, for he gathered them as sheaves into the floor;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.13">Mic. iv. 11-13</reference>. 2. The defeat of this attempt by the vigilance and valour of David, who, upon notice of their design, resolved not to stay till they attacked him, but went in person at the head of his army over Jordan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17">v. 17</reference>), and, in a pitched battle, routed the Syrians (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">v. 18</reference>), slew 7000 men, who belonged to 700 chariots, and 40,000 other soldiers, horse and foot, as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.18">1 Chron. xix. 18</reference>. Their general was killed in the battle, and David came home in triumph, no doubt. 3. The consequence of this victory over the Syrians. (1.) David gained several tributaries, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">The kings,</hi> or petty princes, that had been subject to Hadarezer, when they saw how powerful David was, very wisely <hi type="italic">made peace with Israel,</hi> whom they found they could not make war with, <hi type="italic">and served them,</hi> since they were able to give them protection. Thus the promise made to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>), and repeated to Joshua (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.4">ch. i. 4</reference>), that the borders of Israel should extend to the river Euphrates, was performed, at length. (2.) The Ammonites lost their old allies: <hi type="italic">The Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon,</hi> not because they had an unrighteous cause (justifying a crime which was a breach of the law of nations), but because they found it was an unsuccessful cause. It is dangerous helping those that have God against them; for, when they fall, their helpers will fall with them. <div eID="gen6151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6152" type="x-p"/> Jesus Christ, the Son of David, sent his ambassadors, his apostles and ministers, after all his servants the prophets, to the Jewish church and nation; but they treated them shamefully, as Hanun did David's ambassadors, mocked them, abused them, slew them; and it was this that filled the measure of their iniquity, and brought upon them ruin without remedy (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.35 Matt.21.41 Matt.22.7 2Chr.26.16">Matt. xxi. 35, 41; xxii. 7; compare 2 Chron. xxvi. 16</reference>); for Christ takes the affronts and injuries done to his ministers as done to himself and will avenge them accordingly.  <chapter eID="2Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen6152" type="x-p"/>

entries.06c0d49de558fef940a589f5e926b4fca6746bae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2904"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen4001" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.5">2Sa 10:1-5</reference>. David's Messengers, Sent to Comfort Hanun, Are Disgracefully Treated.<div eID="gen4001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2904"/><hi type="bold">2. Then said David, I will show kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness unto me--</hi>It is probable that this was the Nahash against whom Saul waged war at Jabesh-gilead (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.11">1Sa 11:11</reference>). David, on leaving Gath, where his life was exposed to danger, found an asylum with the king of Moab; and as Nahash, king of the Ammonites, was his nearest neighbor, it may be that during the feud between Saul and David, he, through enmity to the former, was kind and hospitable to David. <div eID="gen4002" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb8466fcb13828a4c54978b9fc14e23956014c42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2905"/><div sID="gen4003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2905"/><hi type="bold">3. the princes of the children of Ammon said unto Hanun--</hi>Their suspicion was not warranted either by any overt act or by any cherished design of David: it must have originated in their knowledge of the denunciations of God's law against them (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3-Deut.23.6">De 23:3-6</reference>), and of David's policy in steadfastly adhering to it. <div eID="gen4003" type="x-p"/>
entries.b375e7794c84c70a0844767bea36ad3c6064f9d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2906"/><div sID="gen4004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2906"/><hi type="bold">4. Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards--</hi>From the long flowing dress of the Hebrews and other Orientals, the curtailment of their garments must have given them an aspect of gross indelicacy and ludicrousness. Besides, a knowledge of the extraordinary respect and value which has always been attached, and the gross insult that is implied in any indignity offered, to the beard in the East, will account for the shame which the deputies felt, and the determined spirit of revenge which burst out in all Israel on learning the outrage. Two instances are related in the modern history of Persia, of similar insults by kings of haughty and imperious temper, involving the nation in war; and we need not, therefore, be surprised that David vowed revenge for this wanton and public outrage. <div eID="gen4004" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec581f430dc4ecbb5612af1ea4fbf8972dc8fed2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2907"/><div sID="gen4005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2907"/><hi type="bold">5. Tarry at Jericho--</hi>or in the neighborhood, after crossing the fords of the Jordan.<div eID="gen4005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4006" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6-2Sam.10.14">2Sa 10:6-14</reference>. The Ammonites Overcome. <div eID="gen4006" type="x-p"/>
entries.d40825d1c29aa940cee181606472cf3c18d266e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2908"/><div sID="gen4007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2908"/><hi type="bold">6-14. when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David--</hi>To chastise those insolent and inhospitable Ammonites, who had violated the common law of nations, David sent a large army under the command of Joab, while they, informed of the impending attack, made energetic preparations to repel it by engaging the services of an immense number of Syrian mercenaries.<div eID="gen4007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-rehob--</hi>the capital of the low-lying region between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon.<div eID="gen4008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zoba--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>).<div eID="gen4009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of king Maacah--</hi>His territories lay on the other side of Jordan, near Gilead (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">De 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen4010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ish-tob--</hi>that is, "the men of Tob"--the place of Jephthah's marauding adventures (see also <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">1Ch 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1">Psa 60:1</reference>, title). As the Israelite soldiers poured into the Ammonite territory, that people met them at the frontier town of Medeba (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7-1Chr.19.9">1Ch 19:7-9</reference>), the native troops covering the city, while the Syrian mercenaries lay at some distance encamped in the fields. In making the attack, Joab divided his forces into two separate detachments--the one of which, under the command of his brother, Abishai, was to concentrate its attack upon the city, while he himself marched against the overwhelming host of mercenary auxiliaries. It was a just and necessary war that had been forced on Israel, and they could hope for the blessing of God upon their arms. With great judgment the battle opened against the mercenaries, who could not stand against the furious onset of Joab, and not feeling the cause their own, consulted their safety by flight. The Ammonites, who had placed their chief dependence upon a foreign aid, then retreated to entrench themselves within the walls of the town. <div eID="gen4011" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5270a216c10c8aa78fe8b80eaa711e380350506: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2910"/><div sID="gen4014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2910"/><hi type="bold">16. Hadarezer sent and brought out the Syrians that were beyond the river--</hi>This prince had enjoyed a breathing time after his defeat (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>). But alarmed at the increasing power and greatness of David, as well as being an ally of the Ammonites, he levied a vast army not only in Syria, but in Mesopotamia, to invade the Hebrew kingdom. Shobach, his general, in pursuance of this design, had marched his troops as far as Kelam, a border town of eastern Manasseh, when David, crossing the Jordan by forced marches, suddenly surprised, defeated, and dispersed them. As a result of this great and decisive victory, all the petty kingdoms of Syria submitted and became his tributaries (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1">1Ch 19:1</reference>). <chapter eID="2Sam.10"/>

entries.275306feb7cb23bf2641c29d66d73d4f03e269e1: <div eID="gen10912" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10913" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10914" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10914" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10913" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10915" type="x-p"/> The king of Ammon being dead, David sends ambassadors to comfort his son Hanun, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sam 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.2">2Sam 10:2</reference>. Hanun, misled by his courtiers, treats the messengers of David with great indignity, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3-2Sam.10.5">2Sam 10:3-5</reference>. The Ammonites, justly dreading David's resentment, send, and hire the Syrians to make war upon him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sam 10:6</reference>. Joab and Abishai meet them at the city of Medeba, and defeat them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7-2Sam.10.14">2Sam 10:7-14</reference>. The Syrians collect another army, but are defeated by David with great slaughter, and make with him a separate peace, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.15-2Sam.10.19">2Sam 10:15-19</reference>.
entries.29fade8bcec597dcd9a293cb187ea6de127ed83d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10916" type="x-p"/> I will show kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash - We do not know exactly the nature or extent of the obligation which David was under to the king of the Ammonites; but it is likely that the Nahash here mentioned was the same who had attacked Jabesh-gilead, and whom Saul defeated: as David had taken refuge with the Moabites, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3">1Sam 22:3</reference>), and this was contiguous to the king of the Ammonites, his hatred to Saul might induce him to show particular kindness to David.
entries.76fcc27a504b9d51081a2f410ff5786598f313ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10917" type="x-p"/> Thinkest thou that David doth honor thy father - It has been a matter of just complaint through all the history of mankind, that there is little sincerity in courts. Courtiers, especially, are suspicious of each other, and often mislead their sovereigns. They feel themselves to be insincere, and suspect others to be so too.
entries.6e1a181d6b304a47c8f77556cd2bcf4c7d562ff7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10918" type="x-p"/> Shaved off the one half of their beards - The beard is held in high respect in the East: the possessor considers it his greatest ornament; often swears by it; and, in matters of great importance, pledges it. Nothing can be more secure than a pledge of this kind; its owner will redeem it at the hazard of his life. The beard was never cut off but in mourning, or as a sign of slavery. Cutting off half of the beard and the clothes rendered the men ridiculous, and made them look like slaves: what was done to these men was an accumulation of insult.
entries.d52f94c68fbcf8d06be7ffad210492af575fee33: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10919" type="x-p"/> Tarry at Jericho - This city had not been rebuilt since the time of Joshua; but there were, no doubt, many cottages still remaining, and larger dwellings also, but the walls had not been repaired. As it must have been comparatively a private place, it was proper for these men to tarry in, as they would not be exposed to public notice.
entries.a1527843c5e23ca12a668908283f4dc7af0b2039: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> The children of Ammon saw that they stank - That is, that their conduct rendered them abominable. This is the Hebrew mode of expressing such a feeling. See <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>. <div eID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10921" type="x-p"/> The Syrians of Bethrehob - This place was situated at the extremity of the valley between Libanus and Anti-libanus. The Syrians of Zoba were subject to Hadadezer. Maacah was in the vicinity of Mount Hermon, beyond Jordan, in the Trachonitis. <div eID="gen10921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> Ish-tob - This was probably the same with Tob, to which Jephthah fled from the cruelty of his brethren. It was situated in the land of Gilead.
entries.9f9949a9d07fad2e2162863b96220f88944f1dbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> All the host of the mighty - All his worthies, and the flower of his army.
entries.d0a07c990de94e1abb98a28a952c227c800603c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> At the entering in of the gate - This was the city of Medeba, as we learn from <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Chr 19:7</reference>.
entries.78b3e9fcdc68904bc5e52caf097648d56046067e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> Before and behind - It is probable that one of the armies was in the field, and the other in the city, when Joab arrived. When he fronted this army, the other appears to have issued from the city, and to have taken him in the rear; he was therefore obliged to divide his army as here mentioned; one part to face the Syrians commanded by himself, and the other to face the Ammonites commanded by his brother Abishai.
entries.10d9b97b7d20004d0a4815d76521f63d8dfdd216: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> Be of good courage - This is a very fine military address, and is equal to any thing in ancient or modern times. Ye fight pro aris et focis; for every good, sacred and civil; for God, for your families, and for your country.
entries.a5a12350be737c09fcca443e6a75674232971b20: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> The Syrians were fled - They betook themselves to their own confines, while the Ammonites escaped into their own city.
entries.6a8b81f38d15cd21d66543e85d9ff67dfd12e556: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> The Syrians that were beyond the river - That is, the Euphrates. <div eID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> Hadarezer - This is the same that was overthrown by David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sam 8:3</reference> and there called Hadadezer; which is the reading here of about thirty of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. But the ר resh and ד daleth are easily interchanged.
entries.ccf6694998a86f3f89614cf44cc041dc10193ef4: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> David - gathered all Israel together - He thought that such a war required his own presence.
entries.ed403ef1e096f15ab45a136ee5cb677c3b46a30f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> Seven Hundred chariots - and forty thousand Horsemen - In the parallel place, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.18">1Chr 19:18</reference>, it is said, David slew of the Syrians Seven Thousand men, which fought in chariots. It is difficult to ascertain the right number in this and similar places. It is very probable that, in former times, the Jews expressed, as they often do now, their numbers, not by words at full length, but by numeral letters; and, as many of the letters bear a great similarity to each other, mistakes might easily creep in when the numeral letters came to be expressed by words at full length. This alone will account for the many mistakes which we find in the numbers in these books, and renders a mistake here very probable. The letter ז zain, with a dot above, stands for seven thousand, נ nun for seven hundred: the great similarity of these letters might easily cause the one to be mistaken for the other, and so produce an error in this place.
entries.f72f20a5631b6b952f128fe92ca5df4d0ca1a3a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> Made peace with Israel - They made this peace separately, and were obliged to pay tribute to the Israelites. Some copies of the Vulgate add here after the word Israel, Expaverunt et fugerunt quinquaginta et octo millia coram Israel; "and they were panic-struck, and fled fifty-eight thousand of them before Israel." This reading is nowhere else to be found. "Thus," observes Dr. Delaney, "the arms of David were blessed; and God accomplished the promises which he had made to Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference>, and renewed to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.1.2">Jos 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>." And thus, in the space of nineteen or twenty years, David had the good fortune to finish gloriously eight wars, all righteously undertaken, and all honourably terminated; viz. <div eID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> 1. The civil war with Ish-bosheth. <div eID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> 2. The war against the Jebusites. <div eID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> 3. The war against the Philistines and their allies. <div eID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> 4. The war against the Philistines alone. <div eID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10937" type="x-p"/> 5. The war against the Moabites. <div eID="gen10937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> 6. The war against Hadadezer. <div eID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10939" type="x-p"/> 7. The war against the Idumeans. <div eID="gen10939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> 8. The war against the Ammonites and Syrians. <div eID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> This last victory was soon followed by the complete conquest of the kingdom of the Ammonites, abandoned by their allies. What glory to the monarch of Israel, had not the splendor of this illustrious epoch been obscured by a complication of crimes, of which one could never have even suspected him capable! <div eID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10942" type="x-p"/> We have now done with the first part of this book, in which we find David great, glorious, and pious: we come to the second part, in which we shall have the pain to observe him fallen from God, and his horn defiled in the dust by crimes of the most flagitious nature. Let him that most assuredly standeth take heed lest he fall.  <chapter eID="2Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen10942" type="x-p"/>

entries.6ac3169eaf8ce6986fcdea95651be20240308be1: <div eID="gen4356" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">III. David’s Reign in Its Decline - 2 Samuel 10-20</title> <div sID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> In the first half of David’s reign he had strengthened and fortified the kingdom of Israel, both within and without, and exalted the covenant nation into a kingdom of God, before which all its enemies were obliged to bow; but in the second half a series of heavy judgments fell upon him and his house, which cast a deep shadow upon the glory of his reign. David had brought these judgments upon himself by his grievous sin with Bathsheba. The success of all his undertakings, and the strength of his government, which increased year by year, had made him feel so secure, that in the excitement of undisturbed prosperity, he allowed himself to be carried away by evil lusts, so as to stain his soul not only with adultery, but also with murder, and fell all the deeper because of the height to which his God had exalted him. This took place during the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, when Joab was besieging the capital of the Ammonites, after the defeat and subjugation of the Syrians (2 Samuel 10), and when David had remained behind in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>). For this double sin, the adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah, the Lord announced as a punishment, that the sword should not depart from David’s house, and that his wives should be openly violated; and notwithstanding the sincere sorrow and repentance of the king, when brought to see his sin, He not only caused the fruit of his sin, the child that was born of Bathsheba, to die (2 Samuel 12), but very soon afterwards allowed the threatened judgments to fall upon his house, inasmuch as Amnon, his first-born son, violated his half-sister Thamar, and was murdered in consequence by her own brother Absalom (2 Samuel 13), whereupon Absalom fled to his father-in-law at Geshur; and when at length the king restored him to favour (2 Samuel 14), he set on foot a rebellion, which nearly cost David his life and throne (2 Samuel 15-17:23). And even after Absalom himself was dead (2 Samuel 17:24-19:1), and David had been reinstated in his kingdom (2 Samuel 19:2-40), there arose the conspiracy set on foot by the Benjaminite Sheba, which was only stopped by the death of the chief conspirator, in the fortified city of Abel-Beth-Maachah (2 Samuel 19:41-20:26). <div eID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4358" type="x-p"/> The period and duration of these divine visitations are not stated; and all that we are able to determine from the different data as to time, given in <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.23">2Sa 13:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.38">2Sa 13:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.28">2Sa 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.7">2Sa 15:7</reference>, when taken in connection with the supposed ages of the sons of David, is that Amnon’s sin in the case of Thamar did not take place earlier than the twentieth year of David’s reign, and the Absalom’s rebellion broke out seven or eight years later. Consequently the assumption cannot be far from the truth, that the events described in this section occupied the whole time between the twentieth and thirtieth years of David’s reign. We are prevented from placing it earlier, by the fact that Amnon was not born till after David became king over Judah, and therefore was probably about twenty years old when he violated his half-sister Thamar. At the same time it cannot be placed later than this, because Solomon was not born till about two years after David’s adultery; and he must have been eighteen or twenty years old when he ascended the throne on the death of his father, after a reign of forty years and a half, since, according to 1Ki 14:21, compared with 1Ki 11:42, 1Ki 11:43, he had a son a year old, named Rehoboam, at the time when he began to reign. <div eID="gen4358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> This war, the occasion and early success of which are described in the present chapter and the parallel passage in 1 Chron 19, was the fiercest struggle, and, so far as the Israelitish kingdom of God was concerned, the most dangerous, that it ever had to sustain during the reign of David. The amount of distress which fell upon Israel in consequence of this war, and still more because the first successful battles with the Syrians of the south were no sooner over than the Edomites invaded the land, and went about plundering and devastating, in the hope of destroying the people of God, is shown very clearly in the two psalms which date from this period (the 44th and 60th), in which a pious Korahite and David himself pour out their lamentations before the Lord on account of the distress of their nation, and pray for His assistance; and not less clearly in Ps 68, in which David foretels the victory of the God of Israel over all the hostile powers of the world. <div eID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.2">2Sa 10:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Occasion of the war with the Ammonites.</hi> - 2Sa 10:1. On the expression <hi type="italic">“it came to pass after this,”</hi> see the remarks on 2Sa 8:1. When <hi type="italic">Nahash</hi>, the king of the Ammonites, died, and <hi type="italic">Hanun</hi> his son reigned in his stead, David thought that he would show him the same kindness that Nahash had formerly shown to him. We are not told in what the love shown to David by Nahash consisted. He had most likely rendered him some assistance during the time of his flight from Saul. <hi type="italic">Nahash</hi> was no doubt the king of the Ammonites mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1">1Sa 11:1</reference>, whom Saul had smitten at Jabesh. David therefore sent an embassy to Hanun, <hi type="italic">“to comfort him for his father,”</hi> i.e., to show his sympathy with him on the occasion of his father’s death, and at the same time to congratulate him upon his ascent of the throne.
entries.d04234246a315e5feee7450b13edb0a297b7266d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sa 10:3</reference> <div eID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> On the arrival of David’s ambassadors, however, the chiefs of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, <hi type="italic">“Doth David indeed honour thy father in thine eyes </hi>(i.e., dost thou really suppose that David intends to do honour to thy father), <hi type="italic">because he has sent comforters to thee? Has David not sent his servants to thee with the intention of exploring and spying out the town, and</hi> (then)<hi type="italic">destroying it?”</hi> The first question is introduced with ה, because a negative answer is expected; the second with הלוא, because it requires an affirmative reply. העיר is the capital <hi type="italic">Rabbah</hi>, a strongly fortified city (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>). The suspicion expressed by the chiefs was founded upon national hatred and enmity, which had probably been increased by David’s treatment of Moab, as the subjugation and severe punishment of the Moabites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>) had certainly taken place a short time before. King Hanun therefore gave credence to the suspicions expressed as to David’s honourable intentions, and had his ambassadors treated in the most insulting manner.
entries.6b6d6ec0f33a4a303ceb4939950663701e9e1b4f: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sa 10:4</reference> <div eID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4362" type="x-p"/> He had the half of their beard shaved off, and their clothes cut off up to the seat, and in this state he sent them away. <hi type="italic">“The half of the beard,”</hi> i.e., the beard on one side. With the value universally set upon the beard by the Hebrews and other oriental nations, as being a man’s greatest ornament,<note placement="foot">“Cutting off a persons’ beard is regarded by the Arabs as an indignity quite equal to flogging and branding among ourselves. Many would rather die than have their beard shaved off” (Arvieux, <hi type="italic">Sitten der Beduinen-araber</hi>). Niebuhr relates a similar occurrence as having taken place in modern times. In the years 1764, a pretender to the Persian throne, named <hi type="italic">Kerim Khan</hi>, sent ambassadors to <hi type="italic">Mir Mahenna</hi>, the prince of Bendervigk, on the Persian Gulf, to demand tribute from him; but he in return cut off the ambassadors’ beards. <hi type="italic">Kerim Khan</hi> was so enraged at this, that he went the next year with a large army to make war upon this prince, and took the city, and almost the whole of his territory, to avenge the insult.</note> the cutting off of one-half of it was the greatest insult that could have been offered to the ambassadors, and through them to David their king. The insult was still further increased by cutting off the long dress which covered the body; so that as the ancient Israelites wore no trousers, the lower half of the body was quite exposed. מדויהם .deso, from מדוּ or מדוה, the long robe reaching down to the feet, from the root מדה = מדד, to stretch, spread out, or measure.
entries.f07ac69e13f45c796e25295d676232106a620a73: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">2Sa 10:5</reference> <div eID="gen4362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> When David received information of the insults that had been heaped upon his ambassadors, he sent messengers to meet them, and direct them to remain in Jericho until their beard had grown again, that he might not have to set his eyes upon the insult they had received.
entries.92895503e49799c4ddaf0ea6f2a4e36ae3376366: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference> <div eID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> When the Ammonites saw that they had made themselves stinking before David, and therefore that David would avenge the insult offered to the people of Israel in the persons of their ambassadors, they looked round for help among the powerful kings of Syria. They hired as auxiliaries (with a thousand talents of silver, i.e., nearly half a million of pounds sterling, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">1Ch 19:6</reference>) twenty thousand foot from <hi type="italic">Aram-Beth-Rehob</hi> and <hi type="italic">Aram-Zoba</hi>, and one thousand men from the king of <hi type="italic">Maacah</hi>, and twelve thousand troops from the men of <hi type="italic">Tob</hi>. <hi type="italic">Aram-Beth-Rehob</hi> was the Aramaean kingdom, the capital of which was <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi>. This Beth-rehob, which is simply called <hi type="italic">Rehob</hi> in v. 8, is in all probability the city of this name mentioned in Num 13:21 and Jdg 18:28, which lay to the south of Hamath, but the exact position of which has not yet been discovered: for the castle of <hi type="italic">Hunin</hi>, in the ruins of which Robinson imagines that he has found Beth-rehob <hi type="italic">Bibl. Researches</hi>, p. 370), is to the south-west of Tell el Kadi, the ancient Laish-Dan, the northern boundary of the Israelitish territory; so that the capital of this Aramaean kingdom would have been within the limits of the land of Israel, - a thing which is inconceivable. <hi type="italic">Aram-Naharaim</hi> is also mentioned in the corresponding text of the Chronicles, and for that reason many have identified Beth-Rehob with Rehoboth, on “the river” (Euphrates), mentioned in Gen 36:37. But this association is precluded by the fact, that in all probability the latter place is to be found in <hi type="italic">Rachabe</hi>, which is upon the Euphrates and not more than half a mile from the river (see Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xv. p. 128), so that from its situation it can hardly have been the capital of a separate Aramaean kingdom, as the government of the king of Zoba extended, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:16</reference>, beyond the Euphrates into Mesopotamia. On <hi type="italic">Aram-Zoba</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>; and for <hi type="italic">Maacah</hi> at Deu 3:14. אישׁ־טוב is not to be taken as one word and rendered as a proper name, <hi type="italic">Ish-Tob</hi>, as it has been by most of the earlier translators; but אישׁ is a common noun used in a collective sense (as it frequently is in the expression ישׂראל אישׁ), <hi type="italic">“the men of Tob.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Tob</hi> was the district between Syria and Ammonitis, where Jephthah had formerly taken refuge (Jdg 11:5). The corresponding text of the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6-1Chr.19.7">1Ch 19:6-7</reference>) is fuller, and differs in several respects from the text before us. According to the Chronicles, Hanun sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Aram-Naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. With this the Ammonites hired thirty-two thousand <hi type="italic">receb</hi> (i.e., chariots and horsemen: see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference>), and the king of Maacah and his people. They came and encamped before <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi>, the present ruin of <hi type="italic">Medaba</hi>, two hours to the south-east of Heshbon, in the tribe of Reuben (see at Num 21:30, compared with <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference>), and the Ammonites gathered together out of their cities, and went to the war. The Chronicles therefore mention Aram-Naharaim (i.e., Mesopotamia) as hired by the Ammonites instead of Aram-Beth-Rehob, and leave out the men of Tob. The first of these differences is not to be explained, as Bertheau suggests, on the supposition that the author of the Chronicles took <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi> to be the same city as <hi type="italic">Rehoboth of the river</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.37">Gen 36:37</reference>, and therefore substituted the well-known “<hi type="italic">Aram</hi> of the two rivers” as an interpretation of the rarer name <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi>, though hardly on good ground. For this conjecture does not help to explain the omission of “the men of Tob.” It is a much simpler explanation, that the writer of the Chronicles omitted <hi type="italic">Beth-rehob</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tob</hi> as being names that were less known, this being the only place in the Old Testament in which they occur as separate kingdoms, and simply mentioned the kingdoms of <hi type="italic">Maacah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zoba</hi>, which frequently occur; and that he included “Aram of the two rivers,” and placed it at the head, because the Syrians obtained succour from Mesopotamia after their first defeat. The account in the Chronicles agrees with the one before us, so far as the number of auxiliary troops is concerned. For twenty thousand men of Zoba and twelve thousand of Tob amount to thirty-two thousand, besides the people of the king of Maacah, who sent a thousand men according to the text of Samuel. But according to that of the Chronicles, the auxiliary troops consisted of chariots and horsemen, whereas only foot-soldiers are mentioned in our text, which appears all the more remarkable, because according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Ch 18:4</reference>, the king of Zoba fought against David with a considerable force of chariots and horsemen. It is very evident, therefore, that there are copyists’ errors in both texts; for the troops of the Syrians did not consist of infantry only, nor of chariots and horsemen alone, but of foot-soldiers, cavalry, and war-chariots, as we may see very clearly not only from the passages already quoted in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Ch 18:4</reference>, but also from the conclusion to the account before us. According to <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference> of this chapter, when Hadarezer had reinforced his army with auxiliaries from Mesopotamia, after losing the first battle, David smote seven hundred receb and forty thousand <hi type="italic">parashim</hi> of Aram, whilst according to the parallel text (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.18">1Ch 19:18</reference>) he smote seven thousand <hi type="italic">receb</hi> and forty thousand foot. Now, apart from the difference between seven thousand and seven hundred in the case of the <hi type="italic">receb</hi>, which is to be interpreted in the same way as a similar difference in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference>, the Chronicles do not mention any <hi type="italic">parashim</hi> at all in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference>, but foot-soldiers only, whereas in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7">2Sa 10:7</reference> they mention only <hi type="italic">receb</hi> and <hi type="italic">parashim</hi>; and, on the other hand, there are no foot-soldiers given in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference> of the text before us, but riders only, whereas in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference> there are none but foot-soldiers mentioned, without any riders at all. It is evident that in both engagements the Syrians fought with all three (infantry, cavalry, and chariots), so that in both of them David smote chariots, horsemen, and foot.
entries.61a6138e761ec32b5e9dc1745718705647910466: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.7">2Sa 10:7</reference> <div eID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4365" type="x-p"/> When David heard of these preparations and the advance of the Syrians into the land, he sent Joab and his brave army against the foe. הגּבּורים (<hi type="italic">the mighty men</hi>) is in apposition to כּל־הצּבא (<hi type="italic">all the host</hi>): the whole army, namely the heroes or mighty men, i.e., the brave troops that were well used to war. It is quite arbitrary on the part of Thenius to supply <hi type="italic">vav</hi> before הגּבּורים; for, as Bertheau has observed, as never find a distinction drawn between the <hi type="italic">gibborim</hi> and the whole army.
entries.d00cb3e6a54b303b7417d0a2d6edfb13f4bf7c4a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.8">2Sa 10:8</reference> <div eID="gen4365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4366" type="x-p"/> On the other hand, the Ammonites came out (from the capital, where they had assembled), and put themselves in battle array before the gate. The Syrians were alone on the field, i.e., they had taken up a separate position on the broad treeless table-land (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference>) by Medeba. <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi> lay about four geographical miles in a straight line to the south-west of <hi type="italic">Rabbath-Ammon</hi>.
entries.32b14a28b8c0a2100f2f0b709a8ecfd6815a7b37: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.9-2Sam.10.11">2Sa 10:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen4366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4367" type="x-p"/> When Joab saw that “the front of the war was (directed) against him both before and behind,” he selected a picked body out of the Israelitish army, and posted them (the picked men) against the children of Aram (i.e., the Syrians). The rest of the men he gave to his brother Abishai, and stationed them against the Ammonites. <hi type="italic">“The front of the battle:”</hi> i.e., the face or front of the hostile army, when placed in battle array. Joab had this in front and behind, as the Ammonites had taken their stand before Rabbah at the back of the Israelitish army, and the Syrians by <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi> in their front, so that Joab was attacked both before and behind. This compelled him to divide his army. <hi type="italic">He chose out,</hi> i.e., made a selection. Instead of בישׂראל בּחוּרי (the picked men in Israel) the Chronicles have בישׂראל בּחוּר (the men in Israel), the singular בּחוּר being more commonly employed than the plural to denote the men of war. The בּ before ישׂראל is not to be regarded as suspicious, although the early translators have not expressed it, and the Masoretes wanted to expunge it. “The choice of Israel” signifies those who were selected in Israel for the war, i.e., the Israelitish soldiers. Joab himself took up his station opposite to the Syrians with a picked body of men, because they were the stronger force of the two. He then made this arrangement with Abishai (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.11">2Sa 10:11</reference>): <hi type="italic">“If Aram becomes stronger than I</hi> (i.e., overpowers me), <hi type="italic">come to my help; and if the Ammonites should overpower thee, I will go to help thee.”</hi> Consequently the attack was not to be made upon both the armies of the enemy simultaneously; but Joab proposed to attack the Aramaeans (Syrians) first (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.13">2Sa 10:13</reference>), and Abishai was merely to keep the Ammonites in check, though there was still a possibility that the two bodies of the enemy might make their attack simultaneously.
entries.8d1cf2cc513dd57cbf7feedf39a769aa27d73b51: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.12">2Sa 10:12</reference> <hi type="italic">“Be firm, and let us be firm</hi> (strong) <hi type="italic">for our people, and for the towns of our God: and Jehovah will do what seemeth Him good.”</hi> Joab calls the towns of Israel the towns of our God, inasmuch as the God of Israel had given the land to the people of Israel, as being His own property. Joab and Abishai were about to fight, in order that Jehovah’s possessions might not fall into the hands of the heathen, and become subject to their gods.
entries.26166219eabff84ae0fe3829f243064b80cf9c3e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.13-2Sam.10.14">2Sa 10:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen4367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4368" type="x-p"/> Joab then advanced with his army to battle against Aram, and <hi type="italic">“they fled before him.”</hi> - 2Sa 10:14. When the Ammonites perceived this, they also fled before Abishai, and drew back into the city (Rabbah); whereupon Joab returned to Jerusalem, probably because as we may infer from <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>, it was too late in the year for the siege and capture of Rabbah.
entries.f5d17c27fab30a47cab60ed3268c962c53ab174e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.15-2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen4368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> The Aramaeans, however, gathered together again after the first defeat, to continue the war; and Hadarezer, the most powerful of the Aramaean kings, sent messengers to Mesopotamia, and summoned it to war. It is very evident, not only from the words “he sent and brought out Aram, which was beyond the river,” but also from the fact that Shobach, Hadarezer’s general (<hi type="italic">Shophach</hi> according to the Chronicles), was at the head of the Mesopotamian troops, that the Mesopotamian troops who were summoned to help were under the supreme ruler of Hadarezer. This is placed beyond all possible doubt by <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.19">2Sa 10:19</reference>, where the kings who had fought with Hadarezer against the Israelites are called his “servants,” or vassals. חילם ויּבאוּ (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:16</reference>) might be translated “and their army came;” but when we compare with this the חלאמה ויּבא of <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17">2Sa 10:17</reference>, we are compelled to render it as a proper name (as in the Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic) - <hi type="italic">“and they</hi> (the men from beyond the Euphrates) <hi type="italic">came</hi> (marched) <hi type="italic">to Helam”</hi> - and to take חילם as a contracted form of חלאם. The situation of this place has not yet been discovered. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> supposes it to be connected with the Syrian town <hi type="italic">Alamatha</hi> upon the Euphrates (Ptol. <hi type="italic">Geogr</hi>. v. 15); but this is not to be thought of for a moment, if only because it cannot be supposed that the Aramaeans would fall back to the Euphrates, and wait for the Israelites to follow them thither before they gave them battle; and also on account of <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>, from which it is evident that Helam is to be sought for somewhere in the neighbourhood of Hamath. For חלאמה ויּבא we find אליהם ויּבא, “David came to them” (The Aramaeans), in the Chronicles: so that the author of the Chronicles has omitted the unknown place, unless indeed אליהם has been written by mistake for חלאם.
entries.1c90cb1be550c9b3f8b894a33c32c7c95db2f38c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17-2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4370" type="x-p"/> David went with all Israel (all the Israelitish forces) against the foe, and smote the Aramaeans at <hi type="italic">Helam</hi>, where they had placed themselves in battle array, slaying seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen, and so smiting (or wounding) the general <hi type="italic">Shobach</hi> that he died there, i.e., that he did not survive the battle (Thenius). With regard to the different account given in the corresponding text of the Chronicles as to the number of the slain, see the remarks on 2Sa 10:6. It is a fact worthy of notice, that the number of men who fell in the battle (seven hundred <hi type="italic">receb</hi> and forty thousand <hi type="italic">parashim</hi>, according to the text before us; seven thousand <hi type="italic">receb</hi> and forty thousand <hi type="italic">ragli</hi>, according to the Chronicles) agrees quite as well with the number of Aramaeans reported to be taken prisoners or slain, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4-1Chr.18.5">1Ch 18:4-5</reference> (viz., seventeen hundred <hi type="italic">parashim</hi> or a thousand <hi type="italic">receb</hi>, and seven thousand <hi type="italic">parashim</hi> and twenty thousand <hi type="italic">ragli</hi> of Aram-Zoba, and twenty-two thousand of Aram-Damascus), as could possibly be expected considering the notorious corruption in the numbers as we possess them; so that there is scarcely any doubt that the number of Aramaeans who fell was the same in both accounts (2 Samuel 8 and 10), and that in the chapter before us we have simply a more circumstantial account of the very same war of which the result is given in 2 Samuel 8 and <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1">1Ch 13:1</reference>-14.
entries.580fe90e0c606bd37bc7ead250e95ff225baea92: <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.19">2Sa 10:19</reference> <hi type="italic">“And when all the kings, the vassals of Hadarezer, saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and became subject to them; and Aram was afraid to render any further help to the Ammonites.”</hi> It might appear from the first half of this verse, that it was only the vassals of Hadarezer who made peace with Israel, and became subject to it, and that Hadarezer himself did not. But the last clause, “and the Aramaeans were afraid,” etc., shows very clearly that Hadarezer also made peace with the Israelites, and submitted to their rule; so that the expression in the first half of the verse is not a very exact one.  <chapter eID="2Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen4370" type="x-p"/>

entries.e52345260292bd8687b34b7cfcc4bfb23100d3fa:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="10" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND it came to pass after this, that the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 19. 1:</ns0:note> king of the children of Ammon <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Nahash, v.</ns0:hi> 2. probably the same whose Army <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feated and destroyed, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 11. who out of enmity to <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> shewed kindness to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> as it follows; hoping also by fo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />menting the differences between <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> to make way for his future Conquests.</ns0:note> died, and Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nun his son reigned in his stead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Therefore there had hitherto been Peace and Friend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship between <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and him; and therefore the <ns0:hi>spoils of the children of Ammon</ns0:hi> are mentioned <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 12. by way of anticipation, and with respect to the story here following.</ns0:note>, as his father shewed kindness unto me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which he might do, either, by offering him his help, if he needed it; or, by supplying him with Military or other pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />visions upon occasion, or many other ways.</ns0:note>. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants, for <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">the loss of,</ns0:note> his father: and Davids servants came into the land of the children of Ammon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the princes of the children of Ammon said unto Hanun their lord, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in thine eyes doth Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid.</ns0:note> Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? Hath not David <ns0:hi>rather</ns0:hi> sent his servants unto thee, to search the city, and to spie it out <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To observe where the City is weakest, and may soonest be taken. The ground of this suspition was, partly, the Conscience of their ill deserts and carriage towards the <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raelites,</ns0:hi> whose quarrel <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had espoused: partly, the opinion they had of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s policy: and partly, the severity of Gods Law particularly against them, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23. 6. which might easily come to their ears. And they knew <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was a zealous asserter of Gods Laws.</ns0:note>, and to overthrow <ns0:hi>it?</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Wherefore Hanun took Davids servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Partly, that he might compel them to bear a part in their mourning, and that in such a way as was usual with them, but forbidden to the <ns0:hi>Israelites, Levit.</ns0:hi> 19. 27. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 14. 1. which probably was not unknown to them: and partly, to fasten this as a reproach upon them, and to make them ridiculous and contemptible. Compare <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 20. 4. and 47. 2. and 50. 6.</ns0:note>, and cut off their garments in the middle, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> to their buttocks <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This was worse than the former, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> wore no Breeches, and so their nakedness was hereby uncovered. Compare <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 20. 4.</ns0:note>, and sent them away.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 ¶ When they told <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto David, He sent to meet them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He sent them Clothes and other necessaries.</ns0:note>, because the men were greatly a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shamed: and the king said, Tarry at Jericho <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Both be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause this was one of the first places which they came to in <ns0:hi>Canaan:</ns0:hi> and because it was now a very obscure Village; and therefore fittest for them in their circumstances: for it was not built as a City till after this time, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 16. 34.</ns0:note> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />til your beards be grown <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For the want or loss of Beards was esteemed a reproach among the <ns0:hi>Israelites.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> return.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 ¶ And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-Rehob <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Near <ns0:hi>Hamath, Numb.</ns0:hi> 13. 21.</ns0:note>, and the Syrians of Zoba <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Of which see 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 14. 47. and 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 8. 3.</ns0:note>, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of that part of <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> which was under King <ns0:hi>Maachah:</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> was a large Country, and there were divers Kings in the several parts of it. This part was near <ns0:hi>Gilead.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 3. 14.</ns0:note> a thousand men, and of Ishtob <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of the men of Tob,</ns0:hi> the Country where <ns0:hi>Iepthah</ns0:hi> dwelt, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 3. Besides these, they hired others out of <ns0:hi>Aram Naharaim,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Mesopotamia,</ns0:hi> as appears from 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 6. and <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. title. And all these were forward enough to Combine against <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> both to revenge their former losses and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proaches, and to give check to his growing greatness.</ns0:note> twelve thousand men.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And when David heard <ns0:hi>of it,</ns0:hi> he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Chusing wisely to carry the War into their Country, ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther than to expect it in their own.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battel in aray at the entring in of the gate <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To wit, of <ns0:hi>Medeba,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 7. which was a frontier City. See <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 21. 30. This place they chose for the Fight, that they might both defend that City and their Country, whereof that was the entrance, and, if need were, might retreat into it.</ns0:note>: and the Syrians of Zoba, and of Rehob, and Ishtob, and Maacah, <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> by themselves in the field <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That by their numer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Forces they might fall upon the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> on the other side.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 When Joab saw that the front of the battel was against him before and behind, he chose of all the choice <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> of Israel, and put them in aray against the Syrians <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which were the most valiant and expert Soldiers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And the rest of the people he delivered in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the hand of Abishai his brother, that he might put <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> in aray against the children of Ammon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And he said, If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will come and help thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For the preservation of our selves and all our Brethren from that utter ruin which our Enemies design for us. Our War is not vainly undertaken to enlarge our Empire or Glory, but for our own just and necessary defence; and therefore we may hope for Gods Blessing and assistance it it.</ns0:note>, and for the cities of our God <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which are devoted to his Worship and Service, and therefore he will plead their cause against his Enemies.</ns0:note>: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Let us do our parts, and quietly refer our selves and the event to Gods good pleasure, which we have no reason to distrust.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Joab drew nigh, and the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, unto the battel against the Syri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He prudently falls upon them first, because they were but mercenaries, and not concerned so much in the Success as the <ns0:hi>Ammonites</ns0:hi> were, all whose interest lay at stake; and therefore not likely to venture too far in their defence.</ns0:note>: and they fled before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">In whose numbers and prowess they had the most con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fidence.</ns0:note>, then fled they also before Abishai, and entred into the city: so Joab return<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from the children of Ammon <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Not judging it convenient or safe to pursue them; because the Forces were not utterly ruined, but onely di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spersed and put to flight, and so might easily rally toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:note>, and came to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 ¶ And when the Syrians saw that they were smitten before Israel, they gathered themselves to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Partly, to wipe out the stain of Cowardize which they had now contracted: partly, to prevent that vengeance which they supposed <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> would execute upon them for their last attempt: and partly, to shake off the Yoke that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had lately put upon them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Hadarezer <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The same with <ns0:hi>Hadadezer, chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 3.</ns0:note> sent, and brought out the Syrians that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> beyond the river <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who having engaged themselves in the former expedition, as was noted before, were now obliged to proceed in their own defence, being also perswaded and hired to this second Expedition, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>: and they came to Helam; and Shobach <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Shophack,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 16.</ns0:note> the captain of the host of Hadarezer <ns0:hi>went</ns0:hi> before them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:254" />17 And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Chosen and Valiant Men pickt out of all <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> together, and passed over Jordan, and came to Helam: and the Syrians set themselves in aray against David, and fought with him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And the Syrians fled before Israel, and Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid slew <ns0:hi>the men of</ns0:hi> seven hundred chariots <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>seven hundred chariots: i. e.</ns0:hi> The Men belonging to them, that Fought in, or with them; as plainly appears, 1. Because the Men onely, and not the Chariots were capa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble of being killed, as these are said to have been. 2. Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it is thus explained in the Book of <ns0:hi>Chronicles,</ns0:hi> which was written after this Book, for this end, to Explain what was dark or doubtful, and to supply what was omitted here; where instead of these Words, are <ns0:hi>seven thousand men</ns0:hi> which Fought <ns0:hi>in Chariots,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 18. And this is a very common Metonymy; of which, See above <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 4. and the Notes on 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 5. Although there might be 7000 Chariots in all, whereof 700 were <ns0:hi>chosen</ns0:hi> ones; accor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding to the distinction made <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 14. 7.</ns0:note> of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For which in 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 18. is <ns0:hi>forty thousand footmen.</ns0:hi> Which may be reconciled divers ways. 1. Both these may be true, that he slew 40000 Horsemen, which being the most conside<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable part and strength of the Army, it might seem suffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient to name them, and every one could easily understand, that the Footmen in that case were certainly cut off; and that he slew also 40000 Footmen, as is said 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> where he mentions them onely, because they were omitted in 2. <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> and the Horsemen being expressed here, it was needless to repeat them in 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 2. The Horsemen may be here called <ns0:hi>footmen,</ns0:hi> in opposition to those that Fought in Chariots; because they sometimes Fought on Horseback, and sometimes came down from their Horses, and Fought on Foot, when the place of the Battel was more commo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dious for Footmen, than for Horsemen; which it is not improbable was their Case here; for <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> being a Soldier of great Prudence and Experience, and understanding the great Numbers of the <ns0:hi>Syrian</ns0:hi> Horsemen; whereas the <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raelites</ns0:hi> had but very few, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 17. 16. would doubtless en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavour to chuse a place as inconvenient for their Horse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men as he could. 3. Peradventure the <ns0:hi>Syrians</ns0:hi> designed to bring the War into <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Country, and therefore hastned their March, and for that end put their Footmen on Horse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />back, (as hath been frequently done in like Cases) who, when they came to the place of the Battel, came down from their Horses, and Fought on Foot. So there is no need of acknowledging an error of the Scribe in the Sacred Text: which, yet if it were granted in such Historical Passages of no moment to the Doctrine of Faith and good Life, it would not shake the Foundation of our Faith in matters of great Importance, which it might reasonably be presumed the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidence of God would more watchfully preserve from all de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pravation or Corruption.</ns0:note>, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And when all the kings <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> servants to Hadarezer <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, for that time, or in that Expedition to which <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e hired them.</ns0:note> saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them: So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more.</ns0:p>
